title: Caro-Kann Defense
description: The opening that made Levy famous. An absolutely fantastic defense for Black which you can play up the entire rating ladder. Pair this opening with Levy's Caro-Kann playlist on YouTube, as well as the "bonus" course here on Chessly.

2rqk2r/pp2bppp/2n1p3/3pPn2/3P2b1/P1N1BN2.text:
We'll continue with 11...Rc8, completing our development. 

If h3, we'll take on f3 and play ...Bg5.

We also have the thematic ideas of ...f6, a common resource in these structures to break apart the center, as well as improving the knight to c4 via a5.

r1b1kbnr/p3pppp/1qp5/2ppP3/3P4/2P5/PP1B1.text:
We calmly retreat to remove any possible discoveries. 

White will have trouble defending the b2- and d4-pawns. 

Our focus is also on completing development and getting our king to safety.

r1b1kbnr/p3pppp/2p5/q1ppP3/3P4/2P5/PP1B1.text: White breaks the pin by playing 7.Bd2, placing the bishop on the same diagonal as our queen.

r1b1kbnr/pp2pppp/2B5/q1ppP3/3P4/2P5/PP3P.text:
White trades the bishop for the knight, the most logical move.

We recapture with 6...bxc6, and now have ideas of ...Ba6, which would prevent White from castling.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2n4p/2ppP3/3P4/2P2N2/PP.text:
The most common move for White is 7.Nf3, supporting the d4-pawn. 

We continue developing with 7...Bg4, pinning the knight to the queen.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n4B/2ppP3/3P4/2P5/PP3P.text:
White can capture our knight, justifying giving up their dark-squared bishop to damage our structure. 

We simply recapture with 6...gxh6, accepting doubled pawns but gaining the bishop pair.

r1bqkbnr/pp2ppp1/2n5/3pP2p/3P1P2/5N2/PP4.text:
White continues developing the knight.

We play 6...Bg4, pinning the knight and following our plan.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/1BppP3/3P4/2P5/PP3P.text:
White develops their bishop to b5, pinning our knight to the king.

It's the second most popular move, played 16% of the time.

We'll force White to make a decision with their bishop by attacking it with 5...Qa5, and pin the c3-pawn to the king as well.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2ppP3/3P1P2/2P5/PP4.text:
With 5.f4, White reinforces the center but neglects development, a move seen in 11% of games. 

Our response is to trade in the center with 5...cxd4 and then win the battle for the light squares.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2ppP3/3P4/2P1B3/PP3.text:
Another option is for White to play 5.Be3, a logical developing move to maintain control of the d4-pawn.

In this position, we choose a slightly unusual move, 5...Nh6.

We are aiming to target the dark-squared bishop by maneuvering to either g4 or f5.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2ppP3/3P4/2P2N2/PP3.text:
The most common move here is 5.Nf3, played in about 55% of games, developing the kingside and reinforcing central control. 

Our response is to soften the d4-square by exchanging in the center with 5...cxd4.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3pP3/3P1P2/8/PP4PP/.text:
White recaptures.

We immediately start seizing the light squares with 6...h5, with ideas of ...Bg4 and preparing the h6-square for the knight to maneuver to f5.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3pP3/3P4/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
White recaptures and keeps their central pawn chain intact, but d4 has now become a target for the rest of the game. 

We can now activate our bishop outside the pawn chain by developing to g4 and pinning the knight with 6...Bg4.

r2qk2r/pp2bppp/2n1p3/3pPn2/3P2b1/P1N1BN2.text: White plays 11.a3, preparing b4 and preventing our knight from jumping to b4.

r2qkb1r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/3pP3/3P2b1/2N2N2/P.text:
White keeps developing, bringing the other knight to c3.

We complete our knight maneuver with 9...Nf5, threatening to capture the knight and then on d4, while also freeing the e7-square for our dark-squared bishop.

r2qkb1r/pp2pp1p/2n4p/2ppP3/3P2b1/2P2N2/P.text:
As seen in other positions, White usually breaks this pin by developing the light-squared bishop. 

We exchange our light-squared bishop for the knight, weakening d4.

r2qkb1r/pp2pp1p/2n4p/2ppP3/3P4/2P2B2/PP3.text:
White recaptures with the bishop. 

We now consolidate our structure with 9...e6 and protect the c5-pawn with our bishop.

r2qkb1r/pp3p1p/2n1p2p/2ppP3/3P4/2P2B2/PP.text:
White brings their king to safety.

This allows us a concrete sequence to gain the advantage, starting with 10...cxd4, creating the usual weakness on d4.

r2qkb1r/pp3pp1/2n1p2n/3pP2p/3P1Pb1/5N2/P.text:
We develop the kingside knight to h6. 

Our plans include maneuvering it to f5, developing the dark-squared bishop, and castling. We may also develop the queen to b6 to target some of White’s weak points.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3pPn2/3P2b1/2N1BN2/.text:
White spots our threat and reinforces the d4-pawn with the bishop.

We continue our setup by developing our last minor piece with 10...Be7.

r2qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2n5/3pP2p/3P1Pb1/5N2/PP2.text:
White unpins by developing the bishop, getting one step closer to castling.

We close the pawn chain with 8...e6, since our bishop is already developed.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3pP3/3P2b1/5N2/PP2BP.text:
White unpins with the bishop, a natural and common continuation that also brings them closer to castling. 

Since our bishop is already outside the pawn chain, we can now close it with 7...e6, preparing to complete development.

r2qkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3pP3/3P2b1/5N2/PP2B.text:
White castles short, bringing their king to safety. 

We’re slightly behind in kingside development, so we continue with 8...Nge7, aiming for the f5-square and adding pressure to the d4-pawn.

r3kb1r/pp3p1p/1qn1p2p/3pP3/3P4/5B2/PP3PP.text:
Our idea is 11...Qb6, targeting both d4 and b2. 

We will finish development with ...Rg8, controlling the g-file, and placing our bishop on e7. 

If we castle, we'll probably castle queenside.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White places a second pawn in the center with 2.d4, the best and most common move. 

We respond with 2...d5, contesting the center on the light squares.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
3.e5 is played 40% of the time, and it was seen in more than 40 million games!

White resolves the central tension by advancing the e-pawn, gaining space and controlling key squares in our position. 

We challenge this setup with 3...c5, immediately striking at the center.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2ppP3/3P4/2P5/PP3PPP/.text:
White reinforces the center with 4.c3, a logical and the most popular move. 

We continue our development while maintaining central pressure.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the Caro-Kann course!

In this first chapter, we’ll dive into the Advance Variation, starting with the most common move on move 4 - 4.c3. 

The Caro-Kann is a defense against 1.e4, to which we respond with 1...c6, preparing ...d5.

1r1qkbnr/p2B1ppp/4p3/3pP3/Q7/8/PP3PPP/RN.text:
White now takes on d7 with check, trading bishops.

We recapture with the queen.

1r2kbnr/p2Q1ppp/4p3/3pP3/8/8/PP3PPP/RNB1.text: White can also capture on d7 with the queen, preventing us from castling.

1r3bnr/p2k1ppp/4p3/3pP3/8/8/PP3PPP/RNB1K.text:
We recapture with the king. However, with queens off the board and a pair of minor pieces traded, our king remains perfectly safe.

We keep pressure on b2 and plan to maneuver the knight to c6, targeting e5.

1rbqk1r1/p3np1Q/2p1p3/2bpP3/2P5/2N5/PP3P.text:
We continue improving our position by bringing the other rook to the b-file. 

Even though we’re down two pawns, our development advantage is overwhelming, it’s actually hard for White to find a move here.

r1b1kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2p1P3/3q4/2N1B3/PP3.text:
White should try to gain compensation and develop with tempo; 7.Be3 is best. 

We trade queens to avoid placing ours on a bad square.

r1b1kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2p1P3/8/2N1B3/PP3PP.text: White recaptures with the rook, creating the threat of Nb5-c7.

r1b1kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2pqP3/3P4/2N5/PP3PP.text:
White develops their knight to c3, attacking our queen, but leaves the d4-pawn hanging. 

We simply take the free pawn.

r1b1kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2pqP3/3P4/5N2/PP3PP.text:
White develops their knight to f3 to support the center. 

We can capture a key central pawn for free!

r1b1kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3qP3/3p4/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
White develops their knight to c3, a great move, using the pin on the d4-pawn to gain a tempo on our queen. 

We retreat our queen to its home square, and threaten to take the knight on c3.

r1bq1rk1/pp2nppp/2n5/1BbpP3/8/2N2N2/PP3P.text: White develops naturally with 10.Nc3, pressuring on d5.

r1bqk1nr/p4ppp/2p1p3/2bPP3/8/2N5/PP3PPP/.text:
White can continue trading in the center with 9.cxd5. 

This allows us to recapture with the c-pawn, opening the c-file and creating a passed pawn.

r1bqk1nr/p4ppp/2p1p3/2bpP3/2P3Q1/2N5/PP3.text:
White could develop the queen to g4, a clever move that targets the g7-pawn and tries to hinder our development. 

We calmly develop the knight to e7, giving away the pawn since our lead in development is huge.

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/2N1p3/2bpP3/2P5/2N5/PP3P.text:
White usually captures on c6 to escape the threat. 

We recapture with the c-pawn, reinforcing the center and creating a solid structure.

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/4P3/1b1N4/5N2/PP1B.text:
White blocks the check with their bishop. 

We trade on d2.

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/4P3/3N4/5N2/PP1Q1P.text:
White recaptures with the queen. 

We trade again before continuing with development.

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/2n5/1BbpP3/8/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
White continues development and pins our knight to the king with 8.Bb5. 

We support our knight with 8...Nge7, moving closer to castling.

r1bqk2r/p3npQp/2p1p3/2bpP3/2P5/2N5/PP3PP.text:
White goes for it with 10.Qxg7. 

We respond by sliding the rook over to g8, gaining a tempo and offering yet another pawn.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/2n5/1BbpP3/8/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
White castles. 

We do the same, bringing our king to safety.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/4p3/4P3/3N4/8/PP1Q1PPP/R.text:
We are ready to finish development with 12...Ne7. 

The position is equal with a full middlegame ahead. 

We plan to castle short, develop our light-squared bishop to d7, and occupy the open c-file with our rook.

r1bqkbnr/p4ppp/2p1p3/3PP3/8/8/PP3PPP/RNB.text:
White can continue trading in the center by capturing on d5.

We’re ready for this exchange,  recapturing with the c-pawn creates a passed pawn and gives us a strong center.

r1bqkbnr/p4ppp/4p3/1B1pP3/8/8/PP3PPP/RNB.text:
The most popular move for White here is to give a check with 9.Bb5+.

We simply block with our bishop, looking to exchange off our less active piece.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/1N2P3/3p4/5N2/PP3PP.text:
White escapes danger with 8.Nb5, aiming to regain the pawn. 

We are fine allowing this, as it will take time, and instead open our dark-squared bishop with 8...e6.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2PpP3/2P5/8/PP3PPP/.text:
The capture on c5, played 21% of the time, does not trouble us. 

We respond by opening up our dark-squared bishop with 5...e6, targeting c5 while our knight continues to pressure e5.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2pPP3/3P4/8/PP3PPP/.text:
The capture on d5 is the most common one, chosen 46% of the time. 

We respond by capturing on d5 with our queen, putting pressure on White's center.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2ppP3/2PP4/5N2/PP3P.text:
White’s best move is to also develop with 5.Nf3, played in about 26% of games. 

We respond by capturing in the center with 5...cxd4, reducing the tension before completing development.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3pP3/2PN4/8/PP3PPP/.text:
White recaptures the pawn. 

We solidify the center with 6...e6, also preparing to develop the kingside. 

Capturing on e5 too early would be a mistake - we’re still undeveloped, and it would allow White to seize the initiative.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2N1p3/3pP3/2P5/8/PP3PPP/.text:
White can also trade knights in this position by capturing on c6.

We recapture, reinforcing the center and building a solid pawn triangle.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2PPP3/8/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
White might trade in the center. 

We recapture with the e-pawn, maintaining pressure on both e5 and c5.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3pP3/2PN4/2N5/PP3P.text:
Continuing development is White’s best idea. 

We also continue developing by bringing the bishop out to c5, gaining a tempo on the knight.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/4P3/3N4/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
White restores material equality with 9.Nbxd4. 

We continue developing with 9...Bb4+, gaining a tempo.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/2PpP3/8/5N2/PP3PPP/R.text:
White develops their knight to f3, defending the e5-pawn.

The c5-pawn has been left hanging, so we capture it with our bishop, 7...Bxc5.

r2q1rk1/pp2nppp/2n5/1BbpP3/6b1/2N2N2/PP3.text:
We continue our development by pinning the knight to the queen with 10...Bg4, removing a defender of the e5-pawn. 

We enjoy a slight edge, with pressure on e5 and ideas of ...Re8. 

The passed d-pawn is also a useful asset.

r2qk1nr/p2b1ppp/4p3/1BbpP3/8/2N5/PP3PPP/.text:
This actually helps us develop. 

We block with our bishop - trading it off is fine, as it was somewhat restricted.

We’ll continue with ...Ne7, O-O, and aim to create counterplay down the open b- and c-files.

r2qkbnr/p2b1ppp/4p3/1B1pP3/Q7/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
Instead of trading, White could increase the pressure by developing the queen to a4.

However, this isn’t a good idea, it only helps us activate our pieces by sliding the rook to the b-file.

r3kbnr/pp1bpppp/2n5/2p1P3/8/2N1B3/PP3PPP.text:
We are behind in development so we need to be careful, that's why we develop the bishop to d7.

This is prophylactic against Bb5, which would not pin the knight, and against Nb5, since it gives the rook freedom to move. 

Our plans include ...e6 and maneuvering the knight to f5 via h6 or e7.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White takes the center with both pawns by playing 2.d4. 

We respond with 2...d5, which is the main idea behind 1...c6.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White advances in the center with 3.e5, their best option, taking more space.

We now counterattack the center with 3...c5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2ppP3/2PP4/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
We’ve now reached the main idea of this second study, 4.c4, a move seen only 2% of the time.

We calmly develop our knight to attack d4, forcing White to make a choice.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In our second study of Chapter 1, we will deal with the aggressive 4.c4. 

While it’s not as common as 4.c3, this move can be scary to face if you haven’t seen it before. 

White starts with 1.e4, to which we respond with the Caro-Kann, 1...c6.

r1bqk2r/4bppp/2p1p1n1/p2pP3/8/3B1N2/PPP1.text:
We develop our dark-squared bishop to e7, getting one step closer to castling.

Once our king is safe, we can consider undermining the center with ...f6, aiming to activate the dark-squared bishop.

Later, we’ll activate the light-squared bishop and seize the b-file with ...Rb8.

r1bqkb1r/5ppp/2p1p1n1/p2pP3/8/3B1N2/PPP1.text: White anticipates our idea and prevents it with 11.Qe2, strengthening control over the f1–a6 diagonal.

r1bqkb1r/p3nppp/2p1p3/3pP3/8/3B4/PPPN1PP.text:
White also plans a knight maneuver, 9.Nd2, heading toward f3. 

We complete our own with 9...Ng6, targeting e5 and freeing the dark-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p1p1n1/3pP3/8/3B1N2/PPP2.text:
White lands the knight on f3, reinforcing the center. 

We play an instructive idea, preparing to exchange our light-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp2npp1/2n1p2p/1B1pP1B1/3Q4/5N2.text:
We push White back with 8...h6 and will also play ...a6, forcing White to retreat or trade pieces. 

We then finish our development and castle.

r1bqkb1r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/1B1pP1B1/3Q4/5N2/.text: White may try to keep us tied down with 8.Bg5, but this won’t work.

r1bqkbnr/p3pppp/2p5/3pP3/8/3B4/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White develops the light-squared bishop, activating it along two diagonals and preparing to castle. 

We create our typical Caro light-square fortress with 7...e6, also allowing our kingside to develop.

r1bqkbnr/p4ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/8/3B4/PPP2PPP/.text:
White castles short. 

We continue developing our kingside with 8...Ne7, intending to reroute the knight to g6.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2N5/3pP3/8/8/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
Capturing on c6 is the main move among experienced players, so White will most likely take. 

Naturally, we recapture.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/1B1pP3/3N4/8/PPP2PP.text:
White proceeds aggressively, developing while adding pressure on our c6 knight with 6.Bb5. 

We simply unpin and protect the knight, leaving White with no follow-up.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/1B1pP3/3Q4/5N2/PPP2.text:
Pinning our knight is the most common move online. 

We prepare kingside development by playing 6...e6, also building a solid light-square formation.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3pP3/5Q2/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
White’s best option is to move the queen to a safe square. 

We prepare kingside development with 6...e6.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/1B1pP3/3Q4/5N2/PPP.text:
White brings their king to safety. 

We support our c6 knight with 7...Ne7 and prepare ideas like ...a6 or ...Bd7 to break the pin.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3pP3/5Q2/3B1N2/PPP.text: White develops their light-squared bishop, getting only one step away from castling.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/3pP3/1n3Q2/3B1N2/PPP.text:
We conclude this variation with an important idea: targeting White’s light-squared bishop. 

This piece is very powerful, as it effectively controls diagonals on both sides of the board.

You will usually continue kingside development in two ways: ...Ne7 for ...Nf5, or ...Nh6.

r2qkbnr/p3pppp/2p5/3pP3/8/8/PPP2PPP/RNBQ.text: White brings the king to safety with 9.O-O.

r2qkbnr/p4ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/8/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.text:
Our kingside pieces need space to develop, so we give it to them with 9...e6.

We simply develop our pieces to their natural squares and place the rook on the b-file. 

Once our development is complete, we will enjoy an edge thanks to a stronger center and an open queenside file.

r2qkbnr/pp1bpppp/2N5/1B1pP3/8/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White captures on c6 with the knight. 

We recapture with the bishop, offering an exchange.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2B5/3pP3/8/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.text:
White accepts the trade of bishops.

We recapture, leaving us with a strong center.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White takes the center with 2.d4. 

We build the Caro chain with 2...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White pushes forward with 3.e5, entering the Advance Variation. 

We strike back in Gotham style with 3...c5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2ppP3/3P4/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
4.Nf3 is our last move to study - an odd-looking move that keeps plenty of flexibility. 

It’s actually the second most popular choice, played in 18% of games. 

We respond by immediately taking on the center with 4...cxd4.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3pP3/3N4/8/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
White recaptures with the knight, bringing it to the center, a move seen in 62% of games. 

We develop our knight to c6, offering an exchange.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3pP3/3Q4/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
White can also capture on d4 with the queen, an unusual move that allows us to gain a tempo. 

We develop our knight, attacking the queen.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the final study on Move 4 sidelines in the Advance Caro. 

Our focus for this chapter will be the natural 4.Nf3 - although not the most common, it’s a very logical move and one of White’s best ideas. 

As always, White starts with 1.e4, to which we respond with 1...c6, the Caro-Kann.

lessons.title: The Pinning Bb5 (5. Bb5 and 6. Bb5)

1k1r1b1r/ppq1n1pp/2n1Q3/1BP1P3/3p4/P1N1B.text:
We calmly slide out of the check with 13...Kb8, reaching a messy position.

White has taken several pawns, but we’ll win a piece in return!

1r2k2r/p4ppp/1q2p3/1b1pP3/1b1P4/1PN2N2/P.text:
We continue with ...Bb5, developing our light-squared bishop and preventing White from ever castling. 

We now have ideas of increasing the pressure on the c3-knight with moves like ...Qa5 and ...Rc8, and White’s position will soon collapse.

1r2k2r/p4ppp/1qb1p3/3pP3/1b1P4/1PN2N2/P2.text: White blocks with 15.Nc3, the only way to avoid losing the queen.

1r2kb1r/p4ppp/1qb1p3/3pP3/3P4/1P3N2/P2Q1.text:
White defends with b3, but this move is a losing blunder since it weakens the dark squares.

We develop our bishop to b4, pinning the queen to the king.

2kr1b1r/ppq1n1pp/2n1Q3/1BP1P3/3p4/P1N1B2.text:
White captures on e6 with check, grabbing another pawn.

Both of White’s pieces, however, remain hanging.

2kr1b1r/ppq1nQpp/2n1p3/1BPpP3/8/P1N1B2P/.text:
White greedily takes a pawn that seems free...

White could also play 7.Bd3, preparing to castle, not a bad move, but only played about 9% of the time.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n4n/2PpP3/5Pb1/4BN2/PPP.text:
This is also the most common move to safeguard c5, but we will use our resources to destabilize White's position.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n4n/2PpP3/5Pb1/5N1P/PPP.text:
7.h3 is a common move to break the pin.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n4n/2PpP3/5Pb1/5N2/PPP1.text:

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/2PpPn2/5Pb1/5N2/PPP1.text:
White castles, a natural move but exactly what we want.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/2PpPn2/5Pb1/5N2/PPP2.text:
White retreats with the bishop.

We respond with 8...g5!, a powerful move that helps us collapse White’s center and one of the most interesting ideas in this study.

r2qkb1r/pp3p1p/2n1p3/2PpPnP1/6b1/5N2/PPP.text:
Although we’re temporarily down two pawns, our compensation is clear.

After 9...e6, our initiative is massive.

We’re sure to regain material on the next move and will keep attacking White’s weak points.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p2n/2P1P3/3p1Pb1/3BBN2.text: But we strike with 8...d4!, attacking the bishop and cutting off its defense of c5, so we win our pawn back.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p2n/2PpP3/5P2/4BQ1P/PP.text:
White develops the dark-squared bishop to e3, defending c5.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p2n/2PpP3/5Pb1/3BBN2/P.text: Developing the dark-squared bishop to e3 is the only way for White to save c5.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2PpPn2/5P2/5Q1P/PPP.text:

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2PpPn2/5Pb1/5N1P/PP.text:
White may try to kick our bishop away with 9.h3.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2PpPn2/q4P2/2Q4P/PPP.text:
But we have a powerful response, 11...Qa4!

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/q1PpPn2/5P2/2Q4P/PPP.text: White blocks the check with the queen, hoping this saves the pawn.

White goes for the critical line, capturing our c5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In this study of chapter 2 we are going to learn how to fight fire with fire...

r2qk1nr/pp3ppp/2nBp3/3p4/3P2b1/2P2N2/PP1.text:
White exchanges their bishop.

r2qk2r/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/3p2B1/3P2b1/2PB1N2.text:
White continues with 9.Nbd2, and so far their development has been excellent.

r2qk2r/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/3p2Bb/3P4/2N2N1P/P.text: White improves their rook, placing it on the e-file.

r2qkb1r/pp1Bpppp/5n2/3p4/1n1P4/5N1P/PPP2.text:
Usually, White ends up trading bishops on d7.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P2b1/2PB1N2/P.text:

White can throw this move in at several points, posing a question to our bishop.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3p4/3P1Bb1/2P2N2/PP3.text:
White defends the d4 pawn with 6.c3.

r2qkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3p4/3P1Bb1/2P2N2/PP.text:
White continues developing with 7.Nbd2.

r3k1nr/pp3ppp/2nqp3/3p4/3P2b1/2PB1N2/PP1.text:
White continues natural development with 9.Bd3.

We develop our knight to f6, controlling the center.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/2nqpn2/3p4/3P2b1/2PB1N2/PP1.text:
White secures their king with kingside castling.

We also safeguard our king with 10...O-O.

r3kb1r/pp1q1ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P4/2P2N1P/PP.text: We continue with normal development, preparing ...Bd6 and short castling.

r3kb1r/pp1qpppp/5n2/3p4/1n1P4/2P2N1P/PP3.text:
White plays 9.c3, kicking our knight away.

r4rk1/pp3ppp/2nqpn2/3p4/3P2b1/2PB1N2/PP1.text: White hopes to control e5 with 11.Re1 and later play Nf3–Ne5.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/3P2b1/2N2N2/PPP.text:
White wisely blocks the pin with the bishop.

We develop our knight to c6.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/3P2b1/3B1N2/PPP.text:
White castles, keeping the king safe.
 
We take advantage of the knight’s development by creating a threat with 6...Nc6.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/2N2N2/PPP2P.text:
There are many different move orders that White can use.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/3B1N2/PPP2P.text:

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Chapter 3, where we dive into the Exchange Variation of the Caro–Kann (3.exd5). 

In this first study, we’ll look at some early sidelines from White, practical moves that may seem harmless but still require accurate handling.

1b1q1rk1/3b1ppp/2r5/8/8/2P1Q2P/PP3PP1/RN.text:
Even though we’re down three pawns, the computer agrees that Black is completely winning after this last rook move.

Our queen, rooks, and bishops combine for a massive incoming attack.

2kr1b1r/pp1q1ppp/8/4n3/4p3/2P4P/PP2Q1P1/.text:
It turns out White’s king is in huge trouble!

2rq1rk1/Q2b1ppp/3b4/8/8/2P4P/PP3PP1/RNB2.text:
So greedy! 

Let's gain a crucial tempo by attacking the queen with our dark-squared bishop.

r1b1k2r/pp2qppp/5n2/2bp4/8/2P4P/PPB1QPP1.text:
White blocks the check with the queen, but we can still tease the king a bit more.

r1b2rk1/pp3pp1/3b1q1p/3Q4/8/2P2N1P/PP3PP.text: White captures on d5 with the queen, their big idea.

r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/5n2/2bp4/8/2P4P/PPB1KPP1/.text:
And we end the variation by castling short.

Our pieces are fully developed, and the exposed king on e2 will give us several extra tempi to keep the momentum going.

There's a good chance we'll get rid of our IQP with ...d4.

r1bq1r2/ppb2pk1/5n2/3p4/7B/2PQ3P/PP3PP1/.text:
We stay calm and play 15...Kg7!

A piece is a piece!

Sacrificing the knight looks tempting since it opens up our king, but we can defend everything and stay a piece up.

r1bq1rk1/pp3p2/3b1n1p/3p2p1/8/2PQ1NBP/PP.text:
Retreating is the safer option, and now we must show that our kingside isn’t overexposed.

White recaptures with the bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pp3p2/5n1p/3p2p1/8/2PQ1NPP/PP4P.text:
White’s capture is forced.

r1bq1rk1/pp3p2/5n1p/3p4/6P1/2PQ1NP1/PP4P.text: White has to capture on g4.

The position is complex but fully balanced.

r1bq1rk1/pp3pp1/3b1B1p/3p4/8/2PQ1N1P/PP3.text:
White takes on f6, going for the d5-pawn. 

We recapture with the queen.

r1bq1rk1/pp3pp1/3b1n1p/3p4/7B/2PQ1N1P/PP.text:

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/3b1n2/3p2B1/8/2PQ1N1P/PP.text:
This is the most logical and also the most annoying move for White, but nothing to worry about.

White also escapes any nasty ...Re8 ideas.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/3b4/8/8/2P2Q1P/PP3PP1/RN.text:
The recapture is forced.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/3b1n2/3p4/8/2PQ1N1P/PP3PP.text:
White castles, a logical choice to finish development. 

We do the same.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/3b4/4n3/4Q3/2P2N1P/PP3PP1.text:
White continues developing, putting pressure on our pinned knight.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/5n2/2bp4/8/2P2Q1P/PPB2PP1.text:
White recaptures with the queen.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/5n2/2bpn3/8/2P2N1P/PPB2PP.text:
White continues with logical development and plays 9.Nf3.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P4/2PB3P/PP3.text:
This move makes sense for White, since we love playing ...Bg4!

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/3pP3/8/2PB3P/PP3PP.text:
White is forced to react, otherwise we take over the center completely.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/5n2/1B1pn3/8/2P4P/PP3PP1.text:
White might be tempted to give this check with the bishop, but it actually helps us develop.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/5n2/3p4/8/2PQ1N1P/PP3PP1.text:
White recaptures. 

We continue natural development, getting ready to castle.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/5n2/3pn3/8/2P4P/PPB2PP1/.text:
Retreating the bishop to c2 has been popular here.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/5n2/3pn3/8/2PB1N1P/PP3PP.text:
White’s best response is to keep developing.

r1br2k1/pp3pp1/3b1q1p/3Q4/8/2P2N1P/PP3PP.text:

r2q1rk1/pQ1b1ppp/3b4/8/8/2P4P/PP3PP1/RNB.text:

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3P4/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In this second study, we go deeper into the critical lines, starting with the cautious 6.h3, a move meant to stop our active ...Bg4.

1r2k2r/p4ppp/Q1nqpn2/3p4/3P2b1/2PB1N2/PP.text:

1r3rk1/p4ppp/Q1nqpn2/1B1p4/3P2b1/2P2N2/P.text:

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/3N4/2PP4/5N2/PP2BP.text:
White develops the light-squared bishop, preparing to castle.

Natural.

White greedily grabs the “free” pawn, gaining a tempo on our bishop, but this tempting move is actually a mistake!

rnbqk2r/pp2pp1p/5bp1/3P4/3P4/2N5/PP3PPP/.text:

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/5Bp1/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
White remains consistent with the plan and captures on f6. 

We recapture with the bishop.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/5np1/2Pp4/3P4/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
White continues developing with 7.Nf3, bringing another piece into play.

The game can now take on a typical structure, where both sides develop calmly.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/5np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2B.text:
Let's examine what happens when White plays several natural developing moves.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/3N4/2PP4/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/2Pp4/3P4/2N5/PP3PP.text:
This pawn push might look tempting for some players, but we’re perfectly happy to see White relieve the tension in the center.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP3.text:

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP3.text:

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
White develops as well.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:

r2q1rk1/pp1nbppp/2p1pn2/6B1/3P4/2NQ1N2/P.text:

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/8/3P4/2NQ1N2/PPP2.text:

rnbqkb1r/pp2ppp1/5n2/2p4p/3P3P/5NN1/PPP2.text: White develops the remaining knight and reinforces the center.

White accepts the challenge and takes the bishop, but they were in trouble anyway. 

We capture the second pawn with the queen, bringing it dangerously close to the white king.

r3r1k1/pp1q1ppp/2pb2n1/3b1p2/2PP4/4B2P/P.text:
White tries to counter by attacking our bishop first. 

We respond with a brilliant desperado, capturing on g2 before advancing the f-pawn!

r3r1k1/pp1q1ppp/2pb2n1/8/2PP1p2/4B2P/PPQ.text: We regain the piece with the pawn push ...f4, keeping the attack alive and maintaining a powerful initiative against the white king.

r3r1k1/pp1q1ppp/2pbbpn1/8/3P4/2P1BN1P/PP.text:
White wisely retreats the bishop to defend h3, but we have another idea. 

We improve our bishop by moving it to d5, disturbing the f3-knight.

r3r1k1/pp1q1ppp/2pbbpn1/8/3P4/2PBBN1P/PP.text:
Instead of addressing our threat, White plays another natural move, but it backfires immediately. 

We have a winning idea: sacrifice the bishop on h3, shattering the king’s defenses!

r3r1k1/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P3n/2P1BN1q/PPQ1.text:
After 16...Nh4!, White is getting mated by force. 

Either on g2 immediately or via Qh2+ and then mate on h1.

A brilliant finish that punishes natural moves with tactical precision.

r3r1k1/pp3ppp/2pb1pn1/8/3P4/2P1BN1q/PPQ1.text:
White tries to defend f3 by retreating the light-squared bishop to e2. The knight on f3 must stay to cover mate on h2. 

But it’s already too late.

r4rk1/pp3ppp/2q1bp2/8/8/2PB4/PP3PPP/R2Q1.text:
We finish development with 13...Be6, bringing out the light-squared bishop and connecting the rooks. 

Our active piece play compensates for the doubled pawns.

rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/7b/2BP4/2P2N1P/PP.text:
Reinforcing the center with 10.c3 is a something White might try. 

We keep up our development with 10...Nbd7.

rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/2BP2b1/5N1P/PPP.text:
White challenges the pin immediately with 9.h3. 

We keep the tension and preserve our active bishop with 9...Bh5, maintaining the annoying pin on the f3-knight.

rn5r/1p2kppp/2pbbp2/p7/3P4/3B4/PPP1NPPP/.text:
We still go for 10...a5! 

Not the only move, but an interesting idea to grab queenside space and prepare a potential ...Na6–Nb4 maneuver.

rn5r/pp2kppp/2pbbp2/8/3P4/3B4/PPP1NPPP/R.text:
White declines the trade, keeping tension on the board. 

If instead 10.Bb3, then ...a5! would be a nice idea.

rnb1k2r/pp2Qppp/2pb1p2/8/2BP4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White trades queens. 

We recapture with the king, which temporarily steps into the open but can safely return to f8 after moving the rook.

rnb1k2r/pp3ppp/2pq1p2/8/3P4/2P5/PP3PPP/R.text:
We actually had a sneaky threat of ...Qb4+ to win the b2 pawn, and 8.c3 is one of the few moves that prevents it, if White spots it! 

We simply castle, bringing the king to safety and preparing ...Re8 or ...Rd8 to activate our rook.

rnb2rk1/pp3ppp/2pq1p2/8/3P4/2PB4/PP3PPP/.text:
White develops their light-squared bishop. 

We continue with an interesting idea, striking in the center with 9...c5 to attack before White finishes development.

rnb2rk1/pp3ppp/3q1p2/2p5/3P4/2PB4/PP2NPP.text:
White develops and defends with the knight, one move away from castling. 

We safely capture on d4, though 10...Nc6 was also possible. We must watch for potential d-file tricks like Bxh7+!

rnb2rk1/pp3ppp/3q1p2/8/3N4/2PB4/PP3PPP/R.text:
White recaptures with the knight.

We develop our own knight to c6, offering a trade.

rnb4r/pp2kppp/2pb1p2/8/2BP4/8/PPP1NPPP/R.text:
White continues with 9.Ne2, controlling f4 and eyeing a future Bf4 trade. 

We keep developing with 9...Be6, a nice idea, since if White trades, we can recapture with ...fxe6 and fix our pawn structure.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/2BP4/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
White castles as well. 

Even if we don’t have the e6- square for our bishop, the g4- square is excellent, we develop there and create a strong pin.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P4/3B1N2/PPP2P.text:
White also castles, reaching safety.

We bring our rook to the open file and prepare a thematic knight transfer toward the kingside.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P4/3BB3/PPP1NP.text:
White continues development, with 8.Ne2, but our plan remains the same. 

We bring the rook to the open e-file and prepare our typical knight transfer.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP1BPP.text:
White castles into safety as well. 

We bring our rook to the open e-file and prepare the typical knight maneuver: Nd7-f8-g6.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pB1p2/8/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R2.text:
White accepts the trade, exchanging our strong bishop. 

We recapture with the queen.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/2BP4/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
White can also activate the bishop to c4, a move that prevents us from playing ...Be6 in the near future. 

We respond simply by castling, keeping our king safe.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/2BP4/8/PPP1QPPP/.text:
White delivers a disruptive check with the queen! 

Instead, 7.Nf3 would simply transpose to familiar territory. 

We don’t want to retreat our bishop or move the king, so we block with the queen. Trading queens is the cleanest solution.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P4/3B1N2/PPP2PP.text:
White plays 7.Bd3, a natural square for the bishop. 

We castle short, completing kingside development.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P4/3BB3/PPP2PPP.text:
White also develops smoothly, bringing out the light-squared bishop to d3, aiming at our h7 pawn.

We get our king to safety by castling short.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP1BPPP.text:
Developing the light-squared bishop to e2 and preparing to castle short is another logical choice for White. 

We continue with castling, completing our kingside development.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2N2/8/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White captures on f6 by far the most often, and it's played in about 62% of games. 

We recapture with the e-pawn, which is a key move that accelerates development.

The doubled pawns will also shield our king later on.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2p2/8/2BP4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White develops actively with 6.Bc4, preventing us from comfortably playing ...Be6 later, one of our most useful developing squares. 

It’s played in about 12% of games.

We respond with 6...Bd6, the standard move in this line, preparing to castle quickly.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2p2/8/3P1B2/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White plays 6.Bf4, a developing move that can’t be bad, but it’s not very common, appearing in only about 3% of games. 

We stick to our plan with 6...Bd6, offering a trade of bishops.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2p2/8/3P4/4B3/PPP2PPP/.text:
White plays 6.Be3, a perfectly reasonable developing move that doesn’t really change our plans. 

It appears in about 4% of games.

We simply continue by developing our bishop to the d6-square.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2p2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
White develops the knight to f3, a logical but slightly inaccurate move since it’s restricted by our f6-pawn.

Still, it appears in more than half of games, so we must know it well. 

We respond actively with 6...Bd6, preparing to castle.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White occupies the center with 2.d4. 

The Caro empire lives on with our standard 2...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
White develops with 3.Nc3, entering the Classical Caro. 

We capture on e4, ready to attack the knight next move.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
White recaptures on e4. 

We continue with the Tartakower Variation, 4...Nf6, developing quickly and aiming for dynamic play.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Our last study covered the alternatives on move five, but now we get down to business with 5.Nxf6, by far White’s most important option. 

We’ll look at all the key continuations except 6.c3, which theory considers best, though the other lines are still very common in practical play. 

As always, White begins with 1.e4, and we build the Caro empire with 1...c6.

rnbqr1k1/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P4/3B1N1P/PPP2.text:
White prevents any ...Bg4 ideas with 9.h3. 

We begin our maneuver with 9...Nbd7, ready to reroute the knight to f8.

rnbqr1k1/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P4/3BB3/PPP1NP.text:
White castles to safety, completing development. 

We do the same, starting the typical maneuver with 9...Nd7.

rnbqr1k1/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P4/4BN2/PPP1BP.text:
White develops the last minor piece with 9.Be3. 

We stick to our plan and start rerouting the knight toward f8 and then g6.

lessons.title: The Main Line 6. c3: White Castles Short or Long

1brqrnk1/pp3pp1/2p1bp2/8/2PP3p/3BB2P/PPQ.text:
We finish the line with a flexible move, 15...Bb8. 

Now White must watch out for ...Qc7 ideas and even the sharp ...g5!? to stop any piece from reaching f4.

2rqrnk1/pp3pp1/2p1bp2/7p/1bPP4/2NBB3/PPQ.text:
A nice idea, aiming to remove a defender of b5! 

Now if given the chance we want to trade on c3 and push ...b5. 

Instead if White runs away with 15. Ne4 we just retreat with ...Be7 and bring ...b5 back to the table.

2rqrnk1/pp3pp1/2pbbp2/7p/2PP4/2NBB3/PPQ2.text: White continues to fight against ...b5 with 14.Nc3, reinforcing the queenside.

2rqrnk1/pp3pp1/2pbbp2/8/2PP3p/3BB2P/PPQ1.text:
White continues their central buildup and places the other rook on the open e-file. 

Both sides are fully developed and ready for plans.

r1b1rnk1/pp3pp1/2pq1p2/8/3P3p/2PB3P/PPQ1.text: White slides the f-rook to the open file, trying to contest it.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1pp1/2pb1p2/7p/3P4/2PBB3/PP.text:
White castles long and dreams of delivering mate on our kingside. 

Our knight swings across for defense with 11...Nf8, but we will soon also launch our own attack.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1pp1/2pb1p2/8/3P1B1p/2PB3P/.text:
Another bishop move is 12.Bf4,  a straightforward idea, as White wants to trade our annoying bishop on d6. 

We complete our knight maneuver with 12...Nf8, following our plan and setting up the sneaky ...Rxe2 tactic to win the e2-knight and the f4-bishop. (Rxe2 doesn't work here, because of 13.Qxe2 Bxf4 14.Qe4! when the h7 weakness proves fatal.)

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1pp1/2pb1p2/8/3P1N1p/2PB4/P.text:
White retreats the queen to d1, returning to the home square. 

It’s a deep idea, though far from subtle. 

We bring our knight to f8, completing the defensive maneuver.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1pp1/2pb1p2/8/3P3p/2PB3P/PP.text:
White plays 12.Bd2, intending to bring a rook to the e-file. 

We complete the plan with 12...Nf8, keeping our king perfectly safe.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1pp1/2pb1p2/8/3P3p/2PBB2P/P.text:
White can also play 12.Be3, aiming to place a rook on the d-file. 

We respond with our usual move, 12...Nf8, sticking to our reliable setup.

r1bqr1k1/pp3pp1/n1pb1p2/8/3P1B1p/2PB4/PP.text:
11...Na6 is an interesting solution since we can’t go for ...Nd7. 

The knight will reroute into the game via c7, then e6 or d5, reaching great squares.

r1bqrnk1/pp2bp2/2p2pp1/7p/3PN3/2PBB3/PPQ.text:
We calmly defend with 13...Be7, securing f6. 

Now we’re ready to kick the knight out with ...f5, having stopped any Nf6 ideas, and follow up with the active ...Be6.

r1bqrnk1/pp3p2/2pb1pp1/7p/3PN3/2PBB3/PPQ.text: White continues maneuvering the knight forward, now targeting our f6 pawn.

r1bqrnk1/pp3pp1/2p2p2/7Q/3P1B2/2PB3p/PP3.text:
We finish the variation with 14...h3, softening up White’s position. 

The position remains highly complex.

r1bqrnk1/pp3pp1/2p2p2/7p/3P1B2/2PB4/PPQ2.text:
White recaptures the piece, trying to keep control. 

We place our bishop on e6, a great square from which it eyes the white king directly.

r1bqrnk1/pp3pp1/2pB1p2/8/3P3p/2PB3P/PPQ1.text:
White exchanges bishops, wisely avoiding the ...Rxe2 trap. 

We recapture with the queen.

r1bqrnk1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/7Q/3P1N1p/2PB4/PP.text:
The queen jumps to h5, keeping active pressure on our kingside. 

We respond by capturing on f4, eliminating the troublesome knight.

r1bqrnk1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/7p/3P1N2/2PBB3/PP.text:
White attacks h5 by placing the knight on f4, but this only leads to a bad trade. 

We capture on f4, and now our upcoming ...Be6 will be incredibly strong.

r1bqrnk1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/7p/3P4/2PBB1N1/PP.text:
White can try to attack the h5 pawn with 12.Ng3, but this leads nowhere.

We defend solidly with 12...g6, reinforcing h5. 

Notice how the knight on f8 neatly prevents any Bxg6 tricks.

r1bqrnk1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/7p/3P4/2PBB2P/PPQ.text:
White plays 12.h3, logically preparing a g4-push to start an attack. 

We keep improving our position with 12...Be6.

r1bqrnk1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/7p/3P4/2PBB3/PPQ1.text:
White plays the solid 12.Kb1, guarding a2. 

We develop our light-squared bishop to the active g8-a2 diagonal, preparing for queenside expansion.

r1bqrnk1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/8/3P3p/2PB3P/PPQB.text:
This is White’s concept, bringing the a1-rook to e1 and preparing f4–f5 to gain space. 

We stay calm and develop with 13...Bd7, looking to connect the rooks and finishing our setup.

r1bqrnk1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/8/3P3p/2PBB2P/PPQ.text:
White brings the rook to the d-file, completing development, reinforcing the center and x-raying our queen. 

It’s time to get our last minor piece into play, so we choose 13...Be6.

r2qr1k1/p2b1pp1/3b1pn1/2pP4/2B2P1p/7P/PP.text:
We finish the variation by placing our knight on g6, reaching a rich and complex position. 

White’s d-pawn is passed but completely blockaded, while the White king might come under pressure in the long term.

Our plan is to place the rook and queen on the b-file to exert pressure on the queenside. We also have ideas of ...f5 and ...Re8.

r2qrn1k/pp3ppB/2p5/6p1/3P3R/2P1Bb1P/PPQ1.text: After 18...Kh8, White’s attack collapses and they lose material.

r2qrnk1/p2b1pp1/3b1p2/1ppP4/2P2P1p/3B3P/.text:
White prevents ...c4 by playing it themselves. 

We capture on c4, opening the b-file.

r2qrnk1/p2b1pp1/3b1p2/2pP4/2B2P1p/7P/PPQ.text: White recaptures with the bishop, a natural move.

r2qrnk1/p4pp1/2p1bp2/1p5p/3P1B2/2PB4/PPQ.text:
And now, push! 

It’s time to launch our attack with 14...b5.

We are aiming to open lines toward the White king and starting the race to see who reaches the enemy king first.

r2qrnk1/pp1b1pp1/2pb1p2/8/3P1P1p/2PB3P/P.text:
White proceeds with the aggressive 14.f4, expanding on the kingside. 

As the old saying goes, “attack on the flanks, counter in the center,” so we strike immediately with 14...c5!

r2qrnk1/pp1b1pp1/3b1p2/2pP4/5P1p/2PB3P/P.text:
White wisely keeps the position closed with 15.d5, obtaining a passed pawn.

We respond instantly with 15...b5, aiming for queenside counterplay and preparing ...c4.

r2qrnk1/pp3pp1/2p1bp2/7p/3P1B2/2PB4/PPQ2.text: White slides the king to b1 to guard the a2-pawn.

r2qrnk1/pp3pp1/2p2p2/3b2P1/3P2Rp/2PBB2P/.text:
White dodges danger with 16.Rg4.

But we strike once more for tempo, trapping the rook with our light-squared bishop, 16...Bf3!

r2qrnk1/pp3pp1/2p2p2/6P1/3P3R/2PBBb1P/PP.text:
Capturing on h4 might look tempting for White. 

After we take on g5, the rook remains trapped with no escape squares!

r2qrnk1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/3b2P1/3P3p/2PBB2P/.text:
White keeps charging forward with 15.g5, still aiming to break through. 

If 15.c4 instead, we’d have played ...Bf3, keeping White tied up. 

We repeat a familiar idea, winning tempi by attacking the rook again, this time with our dark-squared bishop: 15...Bh2.

r2qrnk1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/3b3p/3P2P1/2PBB2P/.text:
The rook escapes to the g-file, hoping to use it as an attacking line. 

We close the queenside with 14...h4, as opening things up would only help White.

r2qrnk1/pp3pp1/2pbbp2/7p/2PP4/3BB3/PPQ1N.text:
White pushes 13.c4, blocking our bishop and making it harder to play ...b5. 

Instead, we stay solid with 13...Rc8, preparing ...b5.

Another idea was 13.h3, when we can play 13...b5. Against 14.g4 we reply with 14...h4, keeping the kingside closed.

r2qrnk1/pp3pp1/2pbbp2/7p/3P1N2/2PBB3/PPQ.text:
Remember, whenever the knight lands on f4, we should capture it. 

So our response is 13...Bxf4, giving our bishop for the knight.

r2qrnk1/pp3pp1/2pbbp2/7p/3P2P1/2PBB2P/PP.text:
White follows through with 13.g4, trying to open lines on the kingside. 

We counter with the clever 13...Bd5, attacking the rook and disrupting White’s attacking plans.

r2qrnk1/pp3pp1/2pbbp2/8/2PP3p/3BB2P/PPQ1.text:
White pushes in the center, gaining space. 

We mirror the idea and “x-ray” the queen with 14...Rc8.

r2qrnk1/pp3ppB/2p5/6p1/3P3R/2P1Bb1P/PPQ1.text: Even a check on h7 with the bishop doesn’t help. There are no discovered checks available, and the rook is simply hanging.

r3rnk1/pp1b1pp1/2pq1p2/8/3P3p/2PB3P/PPQ1.text: We also develop, ready to follow up with ...Rd8 or, even better, ...Re7–Re8 to double the rooks and take control of the file.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P4/2PB4/PPQ2PP.text:
White continues with the subtle 8.Qc2, forming a battery towards h7 and putting direct pressure on our kingside. 

We develop with tempo, playing 8...Re8+.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P4/2PB4/PP3PPP/.text:
White develops with Bd3, placing the bishop on its strongest square. 

We castle short, following standard Tartakower development.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2N2/8/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White accepts the trade. 

We recapture with our e-pawn, getting ready to develop our pieces.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2p2/8/3P4/2P5/PP3PPP/R.text:
The main line arises after 6.c3. 

White’s plan is to follow up with Bd3, Ne2, and Qc2, the most critical setup in modern theory.

It’s the top choice among masters, though in under-2000 games it appears only about 17% of the time. 

We continue with 6...Bd6, keeping to our familiar setup.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White plays 2.d4, staking out the center. 

The battle for central control has begun: 2...d5 is next.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
With 3.Nc3, White reinforces the center in classical fashion. 

We reply with 3...dxe4, giving up some central space in exchange for quick development.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
White recaptures the pawn. 

We continue with the Tartakower Variation, offering doubled pawns for fast piece activity.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
The final study of the Tartakower is a big one! 

Here we face the theoretically critical 6.c3, a line that has sparked intense debate over the past decade among amateurs and grandmasters alike. 

We’ll explore a modern and dynamic approach for Black that can even lead to opposite-side castling and sharp attacking races. 

It all begins with 1.e4, and we answer with the Caro–Kann.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/7p/3P4/2PB4/PPQ1N.text:
Castling short is the safer choice, but by no means worse. 

White avoids an attacking race and instead focuses on solid development.

We continue with our h-pawn push, preventing Ng3 and keeping an eye out for potential ...h3 ideas.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/7p/3P4/2PBB3/PPQ1.text:
White signals an attacking race with 10.Be3, preparing to castle long. 

We respond with the thematic knight maneuver ...Nd7–Nf8, reinforcing the kingside.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/8/3P1B1p/2PB4/PPQ.text: White tries to trade our strong bishop.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/8/3P1N1p/2PB4/PPQ.text:
11.Nf4 is a slightly rare but very intriguing idea. White is actually playing for mate! 

We also improve our knight with 11...Nd7, heading to f8 for defense.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pp1/2pb1p2/8/3P3p/2PB3P/PPQ1.text:
Blocking out ...h3 is a logical response from White. 

We begin our defensive knight maneuver.

rnbqr1k1/pp3ppp/2pb1p2/8/3P4/2PB4/PPQ1NP.text:
A key difference in this line is that White avoids Nf3, preferring to retain the options given by deploying the knight to e2. 

Our response is the revolutionary 9...h5!, a brilliant improvement over the older 9...g6 or 9...h6, both of which gave White attacking chances. 

The h-pawn will now become a weapon in our kingside play, especially if White castles short.

2rqkbnr/1p3ppp/p1B1p3/3p4/3P4/2N2Q1P/PPP.text:
White exchanges on c6, a necessary capture to maintain material balance.

We recapture with the rook, and our plan is to complete kingside development and prepare to castle.

2rqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/1B1p4/3P4/2N2Q1P/PP.text:
White castles short, a logical developing move.

We now play 9...a6, aiming to chase the bishop away so we can capture the d4 pawn.

3qk1nr/1p3ppp/p1r1p3/3p4/1b1P4/2N2Q1P/PP.text: White develops their bishop to d2, supporting the knight and removing the pin.

3qk2r/1p3ppp/p1r1pn2/3p4/1b1P4/2N2Q1P/PP.text:
We continue our kingside development, while maintaining strong pressure along the open c-file.

Our next moves will likely be ...O-O and ...Qc7, adding even more pressure down the file.

3qkbnr/1p3ppp/p1r1p3/3p4/3P4/2N2Q1P/PPP2.text:
White lines up their rook with our king, creating potential threats.

We resolve the issue by developing our bishop, pinning the knight to the rook.

r2qk1nr/pp1n1pbp/2p1p1p1/3p4/4P3/2NP1Q1P.text:
But our bishop is already eyeing the enemy king from a distance.

We continue developing with 8...Nd7, followed by ...Ne7, getting ready for a sharp fight.

r2qk2r/pp1n1pbp/2p1p1p1/8/3PQ3/4B1PP/PPP.text:
We continue developing with 10...Nd7, reinforcing our structure.

This is a typical setup that White aims for in the Two Knights.
White has the bishop pair and more space, but our position is solid. 

We’ll castle and maneuver the knight to d5 via f6, followed by ...b5 to prevent c4 from kicking the knight away.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/2ppP3/3P4/2P1BQ1P.text:
White tries to hold the position together by developing the bishop to e3, defending the d4-pawn.

However, the queenside starts to collapse. 

We begin by capturing on d4.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/2ppP3/3P4/3BBQ1P/.text:
White might think they’re out of trouble after 10.Ne2, defending d4 and avoiding any fork ideas.

But...

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/3pP3/2pP4/3BBQ1P/.text:
We’re just in time to trap White’s bishop!

We leave the opening with a full extra piece and a completely winning position.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/3pP3/3P4/4BQ1P/PP.text: White recaptures with the c-pawn, keeping e5 protected.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P2b1/2N2N2/PP.text:
Surprisingly, the game transposes into an Exchange Caro-Kann, a structure we’ve already examined in previous studies.

This version is very comfortable for us, as we have excellent development.

We can continue with ...Be7 or ...d6, then castle short and look for queenside play with ...Rc8, ...a6–b5, or ...Na5–Nc4.

r2qkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/1B1p4/3P4/2N2Q1P/PP.text:
White can continue by pinning our knight to the king.

We respond by sliding the rook to the semi-open c-file, both supporting the knight and increasing our activity.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/q2pP3/3P4/4BQ1P/PP.text:
Now it’s time for a powerful check with 11...Qa5+! 

Both Nc3 or Bd2 can be met with ...Bb4, leaving White struggling to hold the weak d4, c3, and b2 squares.

rn1qk1nr/pp3pbp/2p1p1p1/3p4/3PP3/2N1BQ1P.text:
White develops the dark-squared bishop to e3, defending the pawn.

We keep developing with 8...Nf6, adding pressure to White’s center.

rn1qk1nr/pp3pbp/2p1p1p1/3p4/3PP3/2N1BQPP.text:
White defends d4 with the dark-squared bishop.

We develop our knight to f6, trying to provoke e5 so we can later reroute it to d7 and prepare ...c5.

rn1qk1nr/pp3pbp/2p1p1p1/3p4/4P3/2N2Q1P/P.text:
White slides the rook to the d-file, trying to prepare d4.

However, it’s too late, as we play ...d4 ourselves!

rn1qk1nr/pp3pbp/2p1p1p1/3p4/4P3/2NP1Q1P/.text: White castles queenside, bringing the king to safety.

rn1qk1nr/pp3pbp/2p1p1p1/8/3pP3/5Q1P/PPPP.text: White is forced to retreat, so 9.Nb1 appears on the board.

rn1qk2r/pp1nbppp/2p1p3/3pP3/3P2b1/2N2N1P.text:
White plays 8.h3, asking our bishop to decide.

We’re happy to exchange it for the knight since it removes one of White’s central defenders.

rn1qk2r/pp1nbppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P4/2N2B1P/PP.text:
It’s time for our typical ...c5 strike, just like in the Advance Caro.

We give the c6 square to our knight, from where it will control d4 and e5, putting pressure on White’s center.

We’ll also castle short, reaching a familiar Caro-Kann structure.

rn1qk2r/pp2npbp/2p1p1p1/3p4/4P3/2N2QPP/P.text:
We continue our development with 8...Ne7, keeping the bishop active and preparing to castle next.

Our other knight will head to d7.

rn1qk2r/pp2npbp/2p1p1p1/8/3pP3/5Q1P/PPPP.text:
We continue development with 9...Ne7.

Our plan is simple: castle short and support the d-pawn with ...c5, also freeing the c6 square for our b8-knight.

rn1qk2r/pp3pbp/2p1p1p1/3p4/3PN3/4BQ1P/PP.text:
White captures on e4.

We recapture with the d-pawn.

rn1qk2r/pp3pbp/2p1p1p1/3p4/3PN3/4BQPP/PP.text:
White recaptures with the knight.

We are forced to take back with our d-pawn, opening up the position.

rn1qk2r/pp3pbp/2p1p1p1/8/3PQ3/4B1PP/PPP2.text: White has no choice but to capture back on e4 with the queen.

rn1qk2r/pp3pbp/2p1pnp1/3p4/3PP3/2N1BQ1P/.text:
White can try the ambitious plan of castling long.

Our reply is to capture on e4, going for simplification.

If instead 9.e5, then ...Nfd7 followed by ...a6 and ...c5 would have given us counterplay.

rn1qk2r/pp3pbp/2p1pnp1/3p4/3PP3/2N1BQPP/.text:
White now completes their fianchetto and can castle either long or short.

It’s time for us to trade in the center with 9...Nxe4.

rn1qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/3P2b1/2N2N2.text:
White occupies the center with 7.d4, reinforcing e5.

We continue developing with 7...Be7, getting ready to castle short.

rn1qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/3P4/2NB1Q1P.text:
White’s most common move is the natural 8.Bd3, but it doesn’t address our upcoming ...c5 break.

So that’s exactly what we play, 8...c5, creating counterplay and freeing the c6 square for our knight.

rn1qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/3P4/5Q1P/PP.text:
White moves the knight back to e2 to allow the c3-push, defending d4 and preparing for ...c5.

We strike anyway with 8...c5, challenging the center and freeing the c6 square for our b-knight.

rn1qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P4/2NBBQ1P/.text:
White can develop their dark-squared bishop to e3 to try to hold the position.

We continue developing with 9...Nc6, pressuring d4 and preventing White from capturing, since ...d4 would win a piece.

rn1qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P4/2P2Q1P/P.text:
White plays 9.c3, building a long pawn chain on dark squares.

We keep the tension and continue developing, while maintaining pressure on White’s center.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3P4/6b1/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Alternatively, White can take in the center with 6.exd5.

This trade suits us, White gives up their central tension, and we simply recapture with the c-pawn.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/3PP3/2NB1Q1P/.text:
Another popular move by White is 7.Bd3, which comes with a gambit idea.

We accept the gambit by capturing first on e4 with our pawn, planning to take on d4 next with the queen.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3pP3/3P4/2N2Q1P/P.text:
White gains space by advancing the e-pawn, also gaining a tempo on our knight.

We escape with 7...Nfd7, preparing to counterattack soon with ...c5, although sometimes we’ll first include the preparatory ...a6.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3pP3/6b1/2N2N2/PP.text:
White advances with tempo using 6.e5, a variation that interestingly resembles the Advance Caro sidelines from Chapter 1.

We retreat the knight to d7, keeping an eye on the central squares.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/8/3PN3/3B1Q1P/PPP.text:
White recaptures with the knight.

We’re now a pawn up after taking with 8...Qxd4, although White will gain time by attacking our queen.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P2b1/2N2N2/PPP.text: White fights for the center with 7.d4.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/4P1b1/2N2N1P/PP.text:
White’s best and most common reaction is to immediately question our bishop, a move played 42% of the time.

We agree to trade and give up the bishop for the knight, since ...Bh5 could lead to dangerous g4 ideas. 

As a consequence, we’ll place all our pawns on light squares.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/4P1b1/2N2N2/PPP.text:
White can try to develop normally with 4.Be2, a move you’ll face about 16% of the time.

We continue development with 4...e6 and ...Nf6, enjoying a solid light-square structure with our bishop safely placed outside the pawn chain.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/4P3/2N2Q1P/PPPP.text:
White recaptures with the queen, choosing not to damage their structure.

As mentioned, we continue placing our pawns on light squares with 5...e6, compensating for the absence of our light-squared bishop.

rn1qkbnr/pp3p1p/2p1p1p1/3p4/3PP3/2N2Q1P/.text:
Playing 7.d4 is a stronger move, immediately blocking the dark-squared main diagonal.

We continue with 7...Bg7, developing with tempo against the d4 pawn.

rn1qkbnr/pp3p1p/2p1p1p1/3p4/3PP3/2N2QPP/.text:
Instead of completing the fianchetto, White should try to block our Bg7 before it appears by playing 7.d4.

We still complete our fianchetto, continuing with kingside development.

rn1qkbnr/pp3p1p/2p1p1p1/3p4/4P3/2N2Q1P/P.text:
Most players in this position blindly castle, allowing us to place a powerful bishop on g7.

So that’s exactly what we play, 7...Bg7.

rn1qkbnr/pp3p1p/2p1p1p1/3p4/4P3/2N2QPP/P.text:
White often plays 7.Bg2, completing the fianchetto, but this is actually a mistake.

We also complete ours, developing our bishop onto the long, open diagonal.

rn1qkbnr/pp3p1p/2p1p1p1/3p4/4P3/2NP1Q1P/.text:
White develops the dark-squared bishop to d2, preparing to castle long.

We also develop our dark-squared bishop, completing the fianchetto.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3P4/8/2N2Q1P/PPPP1.text:
Taking on d5 is a move reminiscent of the Exchange Caro-Kann and is actually the second most popular choice, appearing in about 25% of games.

Players love to capture in the center and relieve the tension. 

We recapture with the e-pawn, maintaining a strong pawn chain with a majority of pawns on light squares.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/3PP3/2N2Q1P/PP.text:
Taking over the center with 6.d4 is White’s most natural and common move (played about 32% of the time).

We counter this by developing with 6...Nf6, putting pressure on the center and keeping an eye on e4 and d5.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/4P1b1/2N2N2/PP.text:
White castles, bringing the king to safety.

As mentioned, we continue with 5...Nf6, fighting for the center.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/4P3/2N2Q1P/PPP.text:
This bishop move, 6.Be2, is the main line at top-level play, even though it’s only played about 7% of the time below 2000 ELO.

I’m a big fan of our solution here, a fianchetto approach. Most players aren’t aware of the best way to defend against it.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/4P3/2N2QPP/PPP.text:
Another option for White is 6.g3, aiming to fianchetto the light-squared bishop, played only about 5% of the time.

Our pawn chain easily blocks that bishop, so there’s no need to worry. 

We respond with ...g6, going for our own fianchetto and placing more pawns on light squares.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/4P3/2NP1Q1P/PP.text:
A common idea for White is to defend the center with 6.d3, a move we can expect to see about 20% of the time.

Since White hasn’t occupied the center, we go for a very interesting idea, 6...g6, aiming to fianchetto our bishop on the long diagonal.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/2N2Q1P/PPP2P.text:
White takes the center with 7.d4.

We develop our knight to c6, attacking d4. 

Our plan is simple: continue with ...Nf6, ...Be7, ...O-O, and look for counterplay on the queenside.

rn2k2r/pp3p1p/2p1pp2/3q4/1b2BB2/5Q1P/PPP.text: White keeps gaining time with 13.Be4, attacking the queen again.

rn2k2r/pp3p1p/2p1pp2/8/1bq1BB2/5Q1P/PPP1.text:
We reply with 13...Qc4+, giving a check.

The game could end in a draw after 14.Bd3 Qd5 =, as the position repeats.

rn2k2r/pp3pbp/2p1p1p1/3q4/3PQ3/4B2P/PPP1.text:
We end the variation with 11...Qd5, forcing the trade of queens.

Our next moves will be ...cxd5, ...Nc6, and later ...Rc8, reaching a balanced and solid position.

rn2k2r/pp3ppp/2p1pN2/3q4/1b3B2/3B1Q1P/PP.text:
White exchanges on f6 with check, doubling our f-pawns.

We’re forced to recapture with 12...gxf6.

rn2k2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4q3/1b2NB2/3B1Q1P/P.text:
White continues gaining tempos on our queen with 11.Bf4.

We calmly slide it to d5, where it sits strongly. 

Our plan could be ...Nd7–e5.

rn2k2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/8/1b1qN3/3BBQ1P/PPP.text:
White’s king escapes the check, and our queen is again under attack.

We keep it active with 10...Qe5, aligning it on the same file as the enemy king.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/8/3qN3/3BBQ1P/PPP2.text:
White develops the bishop with tempo on our queen, a logical move.

Instead of retreating the queen, we throw in a check with ...Bb4+, forcing the king to move and preventing White from castling. 

10.c3 doesn’t work, as we would simply capture on d3.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
White develops the knight to c3, reinforcing the center.

We play 2...d5, as we always do in the Caro-Kann, challenging the center and building our Caro structure.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP1.text:
White develops the second knight to f3, entering the Two Knights Variation.

It's played a quarter of the time.

Our remedy against this solid setup is the main 3...Bg4, as mentioned in the introduction, bringing the bishop outside the pawn chain.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In this chapter, we will study the Two Knights, a solid system that White can play.

We’ll focus on 3...Bg4, the solid main line, but with a slight twist of our own.

You can find an alternative weapon against this system in the Bonus Lines course. 

As always, White starts with 1.e4, and we respond with the Caro-Kann: 1...c6.

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/1qn1p2n/2BpP3/8/2N2P2/PPP.text:
White trades pieces with 9.Bxc5.

We recapture with the queen, and it becomes clear that the e5-pawn is hard to defend.

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/1qn1p3/1BbpP3/3N1P2/2P5/P.text:
White pins our knight with 13.Bb5 to save theirs.

We castle, getting out of the pin and completing development.

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/2n1p2n/2qpP3/5P2/2N5/PPP1.text: White tries to defend e5 with 10.f4.

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2qpP3/5Pn1/2N5/PPP1.text:
That defense isn’t ideal and allows us to create even bigger threats with 10...Ng4, with both the queen and the knight eyeing f2.

Black is winning here as White has no way to defend against the threat.

r1b1k2r/ppq2ppp/4pn2/2bp4/4P3/P2BBP2/1PP.text: We recapture with the bishop, leaving ourselves one move away from castling, with good central control and an easy position to play.

r1b1k2r/ppqn1ppp/2pb1n2/4p3/3PP3/P1N1BN2.text:
We do the same with 10...Bd6, reinforcing the e5-pawn and creating a strong dark-square formation.

We'll castle next with a balanced position.

r1b1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1q2pn2/2pp4/N2PP3/P2BB.text:
With 8.Na4, White goes for a forcing line against our pawn break.

We calmly retreat the queen to c7, keeping everything protected.

r1b1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1qp1pn2/3p4/3PP3/P1N1B.text:
White can also directly protect the b2-pawn with 7.Rb1.

It’s time for us to strike back in the center with 7...dxe4.

r1b1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1qp1pn2/3p4/3PP3/P1NBB.text:
Safeguarding the center with 7.Bd3 is one of White’s ways to handle the position.

We strike with 7...c5, one of the key thematic ideas of the whole ...Qb6 variation. 

This break not only activates our pieces but also exploits the weakness created by 3.f3.

r1b1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1qp1pn2/3pP3/3P4/P1N1B.text:
White has fallen for this trick in a surprising number of games! 

Pushing e5 is a clear blunder.

r1b1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1qp1pn2/8/3PP3/P1N1B3/.text:
White recaptures with the f-pawn, a logical move to keep the central pawns connected.

We push in the center with 8...e5, blocking White's pawns. White cannot capture since the bishop on e3 would be hanging. 

We’ll continue with ...Qc7, ...Bd6, and ...O-O, and eventually take on d4 at the right moment to liberate our pieces.

r1b1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1qp2n2/4p3/3PP3/P1N1BN.text:
White develops the other knight, attacking e5 and defending d4.

We slide our queen back to c7, defending the e5-pawn and stepping out of the bishop’s scope.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1q2pn2/3pn3/3P4/1P1BBP2/.text:
And now comes the blow, 9.Nxe5!, capturing the key e5 pawn thanks to the pin.

We leave the opening a pawn up and with an excellent position.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1p2n/2PpP3/8/2N1BP2/P.text:
White may now decide it’s time to release the tension by capturing on c5.

However, that only helps us speed up development, as we can recapture on c5 with our bishop.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1p2n/2ppP3/3P1P2/2PB1.text:
White develops the light-squared bishop, keeping an eye on the f5 square.

Now it’s time for us to capture on d4.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1p2n/3pP3/3P1P2/3B1N2.text:
White recaptures with the pawn.

We continue with 9...Bd7, a calm-looking move that threatens to capture on d4, since it eliminates any Bb5+ ideas.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1pn2/2ppP3/3P4/1PPBBP.text:
White advances in the center with 8.e5, gaining a tempo on our knight, but this move falls right into our trap.

We begin by capturing on d4, attacking the bishop with our pawn.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1pn2/3pP3/3P4/1P1BBP2.text: White is forced to recapture on d4.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1qp1pn2/3pn3/3P4/P1N1BP2.text:
That’s just a free pawn! 

We capture on e5 with our knight. The d4 pawn is pinned because the bishop behind it is hanging!

r1b1kb1r/ppq2ppp/4pn2/2Np4/4P3/P2BBP2/1P.text: White continues the exchanges, taking again on c5 with the knight.

r1b1kb1r/ppqn1ppp/4pn2/2Pp4/N3P3/P2BBP2/.text:
White captures on c5 with the pawn.

We recapture with the knight, maintaining material balance.

r1b1kbnr/pp1n1ppp/1qp1p3/3p4/3PP3/P1N1BP.text:
White’s whole plan was to play 6.Be3, and now that the b2-pawn is poisoned, they’ve accomplished it.

We cannot take on b2 because of 6.Na4.

Instead, we continue developing with 6...Ngf6, adding pressure to the center.

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/1qn1p3/2pp4/3PP3/1PPBBP2.text:
White keeps reinforcing the center with their pieces, 7.Bd3.

Our strategy is clear: develop and attack White’s pawns.

And there’s even a nice trap hidden in the position.

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/1qn1p3/2ppP3/3P1P2/2P2N2.text:
White continues to develop and defend the center.

We respond with 7...Nh6, a useful maneuver to route the knight toward f5, adding another attacker on d4.

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/1qn1p3/2ppP3/3P4/2N1BP2/.text:
White continues developing and defending d4, this time with 7.Be3.

The problem with this move is 7...Nh6, immediately going after the dark-squared bishop with our knight and increasing the pressure.

r1b2rk1/p3bppp/1q2p3/2P1P3/3p1P2/1NP1B3/.text: White captures on c5, winning the pawn.

r1b2rk1/p3bppp/1q2p3/2ppP3/1P3P2/1NP1B3/.text:
White retreats the knight to b3, trying to use the pin to win a pawn.

We push our d-pawn, attacking the bishop, a powerful counterstrike supported by a tactical idea.

r1b2rk1/p3bppp/1qp1p3/3pP3/1P1N1P2/2P1B3.text:
White develops their bishop to e3, x-raying our queen.

We’re just in time to play 16...c5, blocking the bishop’s view and breaking open the center.

r1b2rk1/p3bppp/2q1p3/2P1P3/3p1P2/1NP1B3/.text:
But we slide our queen to c6, creating a strong double attack that hits both the bishop and the g2-pawn.

Our dark-squared bishop can head to h4 and the light-squared one to a6, controlling key diagonals.

With open files and active pieces, we reach a dominant position to conclude the variation.

r1b2rk1/p4ppp/1qp1p3/2bpP3/1P1N1P2/2P5/P.text:
White tries to push us back with 15.b4.

We retreat our bishop to e7, calmly preparing to play ...c5.

r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/1qB1p3/2bpP3/3N1P2/2P5/PP.text:
White exchanges their bishop for our knight, as otherwise we’d capture on d4.

We recapture with the b-pawn, opening the diagonal for our light-squared bishop.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2ppP3/3P1P2/2P5/PP.text:
White’s next move defends e5 and prepares the f3-square for the knight.

It’s time for our common queen move, 6...Qb6, increasing the pressure on d4 and preventing the dark-squared bishop from developing.

r3kb1r/pp1b1pp1/1q2p3/3pPn1p/3P1P2/2NQ1N.text:
We play a nice idea, preventing any g4-pushes that would kick our knight away from f5.

Next, we’ll finish development with ...Be7 and ...O-O, followed by ...Rc8, giving us strong queenside play.

r3kb1r/pp1b1ppp/1q2p2n/3pP3/1n1P1P2/2N2N.text:
White develops the other knight.

We capture on c2, gaining the bishop pair advantage.

r3kb1r/pp1b1ppp/1q2p2n/3pP3/3P1P2/2N2N2/.text:
White recaptures with the queen.

Now that the light-squared bishop is gone, we occupy the f5-square with our knight, adding another attacker to d4.

r3kb1r/pp1b1ppp/1q2p3/3pPn2/3P1P2/2NQ1N2.text: White defends the pawn with the queen.

r3kb1r/pp1b1ppp/1qn1p2n/3pP3/3P1P2/5N2/P.text:
White’s bishop retreats, and now the d4-pawn is reinforced.

We go after White’s strong bishop with 10...Nb4.

rnb1k2r/pp3ppp/1q2p3/2bpP3/3N1P2/2P5/PP4.text:
White defends the knight with 12.c3, reinforcing it with the pawn.

We continue developing while adding pressure on d4, bringing the knight to c6.

rnb1k2r/pp3ppp/2q1p3/2bpP3/3N1P2/8/PPP3P.text:
White tries to block the diagonal with 11.Nd4, which also frees their light-squared bishop for development.

We move our queen to b6, adding pressure to d4.

rnb1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1q2p3/2ppP3/N2P1P2/8/P.text:
White plays 8.Na4, trying to chase our queen away.

We slide our queen to c6, attacking the knight.

rnb1kbnr/pp3ppp/1q2p3/2pp4/3PP3/1PP1BP2/.text:

rnb1kbnr/pp3ppp/1qp1p3/3p4/3PP3/2N2P2/PP.text:

rnb1kbnr/pp3ppp/1qp1p3/3pP3/3P4/2N2P2/PP.text:

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/3PP3/2N2P2/PPP.text:
White’s most common option, played 42% of the time, is to develop and support the e4-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/3P4/5P2/PPP3P.text:

We calmly continue with 10...b6 instead, nice and slow.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/5n2/1B1P4/8/2N5/PP1P1P.text:

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/5n2/3P4/Q7/2N5/PP1P1PP.text:

White might think that trading queens after 7.dxe4 brings some relief.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3pP3/3P4/8/PP3PPP/R.text:

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3pPb2/3P4/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
White develops logically with 6.Nc3.

r2qkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3pP3/3P2b1/2N2N2/PP.text:
We respond with the strong 7...Bg4, losing a tempo but creating a powerful pin.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/6p1/3n4/8/2N2N2/PP1P1PP.text: We end the variation by preparing our fianchetto and castling, just like in the Panov!

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2P2n2/8/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP/.text:
White shouldn’t accept the gambit, it was better to play 4.d4 or Nc3.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/1B1P4/8/8/PP1P1PPP/.text:

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3P4/8/2N5/PP1P1PPP/.text:
5.Nc3 often transposes into the Panov, and it's played about 64% of the time.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/8/3n4/8/2N2N2/PP1P1PPP/.text:
White continues with natural development, 6.Nf3.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/2P1P3/8/PP1P1PPP.text:

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3P4/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP/.text:

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3P4/4P3/8/PP1P1PPP/.text:

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3P4/8/8/PP1P1PPP/RNBQ.text:

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3pP3/8/8/PP1P1PPP/RNB.text:
Pushing the e-pawn leads to a strange version of the Advance Caro-Kann, but it’s played about 15% of the time.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:

White fianchettos the light-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3pP3/8/PPPPQPPP/R.text:
